subsubtopic: EFFECT OF REGULATION CHANGE ON CANADIAN ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me share with you a letter from a constituent who explains just how unfair and wrong is the Government. The letter reads as follows:
The logic of relating pension benefits, paid for and earned by a worker in a previous position, to unemployment insurance benefits to which the worker is otherwise entitled eludes me.
I am a retired member of the Canadian Forces drawing an annuity. I am, and have been since my retirement employed fulltime in a job in the private sector. I pay the same unemployment insurance premiums as other workers earning the same salary. In the event I left this employment-for whatever reason-the fact that I am drawing a pension from a previous career should have no bearing on my unemployment insurance benefits.
In effect, this proposal would force me and others in my position to pay a premium for a benefit to which I would not be entitled. It seems to me that this is hardly free enterprise thinking.
I might point out that serving members of the Canadian Forces pay full unemployment insurance premiums and this proposal could have a serious effect on many members who are forced to retire as early as age 50 and may well have no entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits, despite the fact that they have paid premiums for 20 or more years.
It is unlikely that much can be done to stop this proposal, as our current majority Government's cavalier treatment of the individual and the individual's rights seems cast in concrete.

It has been over 14 months now since the Minister made that promise. Approximately two-thirds of the workers at Stelco's Griffith iron ore mine have already been permanently laid off, with the rest to get the axe between now
and April, and this in spite of a major tax remission granted to Stelco by the then PC provincial Government.
Moreover, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on November 8, 1984, announced that he would be providing tax relief for people facing plant closures, particularly in single-industry towns. Income tax time is approaching and the people of Ear Falls wonder whether the Minister of Finance will come through on his promise. The Minister has had the Ear Falls situation under study for months. The people of Ear Falls need and deserve an answer. They need it now.

subsubtopic: DEATH OF MONCTON BOY DESPITE COMMUNITY'S EFFORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to bring to the attention of the House the life struggle of a young boy and the response of Canadians to this human tragedy.
One-year-old Patrick Drisdelle of Moncton died Sunday in Boston after a valiant community effort to raise funds to provide the necessary medical care for a successful liver transplant. Although a donor was found, two subsequent operations were necessary and the liver failed to function, leading to the tragic end of a long and hard-fought battle.
I am sure other Members of the House join with me in expressing our sympathy to Roland and Cheryl Drisdelle and their family. Patrick's fight for life leaves me and others torn between feelings of sadness and pride, sadness because, despite the best efforts of all, Patrick's struggle was lost. The feeling of pride emanates from the tremendous moral and financial support provided by the people of Greater Moncton and throughout Canada. This tragedy has once again brought the kindness and compassion of Canadians to the fore. I take particular pride in the response of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). Not only did he call personally to express his condolences, he also facilitated immediate arrangements by providing staff assistance and transportation to the family.
Mr. Prime Minister, I appreciate your thoughtfulness, which I know expressed to the Drisdelle family the thoughts of a number of Canadians who shared their grief. Your understanding and sympathy exemplified the sorrow felt by many who were touched by Patrick's fight for life. Your actions, and those of the many people involved in Patrick's struggle, reaffirm the ability of the Canadian people to open their hearts in a united effort on behalf of a child in need.

Mr. Speaker, the most recent report of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, or OECD, shows that the Canadian economy is more healthy than that of most Western countries. This powerful international economic organization published its latest report in mid-December 1985. The major points are as follows:
Canada is ranked first among the 25 member countries of the OECD in the area of job creation.
Based on our job creation figures, the OECD concludes that unemployment should continue on its downward trend in 1986.
Canada is ranked second out of 25 for individual purchasing power, its performance being exceeded only by that of the United States.
The competitivity of our country has greatly improved vis-avis the United States.
Contrary to many European countries, Canada is not affected by a discrepancy between manpower costs and productivity, which means that wage increases reflect productivity increases.
February 5, 1986

According to the OECD economists, the deficit has been under control since the budget was brought down last May and it will still be under control at the end of February.
The report also foresees sustained growth in the export sector following an increase in automobile, paper and natural gas sales. This last increase, say the experts, is due to the implementation of the Western Accord signed recently by the Conservatives.
Mr. Speaker, there are grounds for rejoicing in the figures published by the OECD. Canada is truly on the right track. This is something that the population should know.
To conclude, I wish to point out that we, in Beauce, are buoyed up by feelings of optimism, trust in the future and confidence.

The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-65, an Act to amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act and other Acts in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from a Legislative Committee.

There are eleven report stage amendment motions listed on today's Order Paper concerning Bill C-65, an Act to amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act and other Acts in consequence thereof.
The Chair has examined the motions and found them procedurally acceptable, except one, namely Motion No. 5 in the name of the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson).
Motions Nos. 1 and 2 will be debated and voted on separately.
Motions Nos. 3, 4, 6 and 7 will be grouped for debate and voted on separately.

Motion No. 5 seeks to introduce a new concept into the Bill, that of collective bargaining, which is clearly beyond the scope of the Bill. I refer the Hon. Member to the Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, Citation 773(1).
In addition, the motion tries to bring in provisions of the Public Service Staff Relations Act, which specifically excludes members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and by so
doing indirectly tries to broaden the scope of that Act. As the Hon. Member knows, Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, Citation 773(8)(a) clearly states that this cannot be done. Therefore, I must rule the motion out of order.

Motions Nos. 8, 9, 10 and 11 will be debated and voted on separately.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to put forward very briefly my concerns with respect to Motions Nos. 9 and 11 with respect to the preliminary ruling made by the Chair.
Having reviewed the report stage, I just want to question, if I may, the procedural acceptability of these motions. Motion No. 9 standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) appears to broaden the nature of complaints to include those about "the activities of the Force in general".
Since the clause in question deals with the actions of specific individuals and not of the Force, it is hard to see how it is relevant to the clause. I would find it difficult to think of a way of complaining about an activity of an inanimate organization without having a complaint against a member of that organization.
Our past practice in this regard, as outlined in Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, Citation 773(1) is as follows: "An amendment is out of order if it is irrelevant to the Bill or beyond its scope". Therefore, I would argue that the motion is irrelevant to the Bill and ought not to be put to the House.
Motion No. 11 seeks to ensure that the Public Complaints Commission has the final decision in the case of appeals from the public with respect to members of the RCM Police. You will be aware, Mr. Speaker, that the House agreed in principle to granting this power to the Commissioner of the RCM Police when it agreed to the Bill at second reading.
In light of this, Mr. Speaker, I think you might find that the motion is contrary to this principle and ought not to be put to the House if we are to be consistent with the practice which is amply outlined in Citation 773(2) of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, which reads as follows:
An amendment must not be inconsistent with, or contradictory to, the Bill as so far agreed to-
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to respond to the suggestion which was made with respect to Motions Nos. 9 and 11, and comment briefly with respect to Your Honour's preliminary ruling on Motion No. 5.
First, with respect to the comments of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) on Motion No. 9, the clause in question seeks to introduce a new Section 45.35 of the RCMP Act which is headed "Public Complaints". That section sets out a mechanism for the receipt of complaints by members of the public who certainly could complain either with respect to the specific conduct of an individual member of the RCMP or, indeed, might very well wish to complain in a more general

sense about particular operational policies, for example, of the RCMP.
I would note that a predecessor Bill, Bill C-50, given first reading in April of 1978, with a similar provision, made reference to the activities of the Force in general. Therefore, I suggest to my colleague, the President of the Privy Council, that this is well within the scope of the particular clause proposed for amendment.
With respect to Motion No. 11, once again this seeks to extend certain provisions of this Bill. As it is now worded, the Bill would establish a mechanism whereby there would be a Public Complaints Commission which could hold a hearing and make recommendations to the Commission.
This amendment was discussed at great length in committee and is well within the scope of the clause it seeks to amend because it would merely include the additional step, as it were, of allowing a final appeal and decision by the Public Complaints Commission. I suggest that Your Honour's ruling is certainly well within the scope of this particular motion.
Finally on that point, when the House adopted the Bill at second reading it adopted the broad principles of the legislation. It would be inaccurate to suggest that the House adopted in principle a whole series of individual clauses. Surely the job of the committee is to examine the representations made by witnesses and make improvements in the legislation. If one if unsuccessful, then at report stage, one should make an effort to improve the Bill again on a serious question such as this. That, after all, is the purpose of report stage.
With respect to Your Honour's preliminary ruling on Motion No. 5, I respectfully suggest that Your Honour reconsider this particular matter. It suggested that the motion seeks to introduce a new concept into the Bill, that of collective bargaining. However, the Bill itself very clearly deals with the whole question of the nature of the relationship between the 14,000 members of the RCMP and their employer. This proposed motion would provide an alternative to the mechanism established in the Bill. It is not fundamentally different in principle; rather, it is once again an attempt to incorporate in the Bill, through changes to two other pieces of legislation, the representations made by, in particular, the Association of 17 Divisions seeking the right to collective bargaining, which is currently denied to members of the Force. Therefore I hope that on reflection perhaps Your Honour might see fit to allow Motion No. 5 to be in order and debated as well.

Motion No. 1
That Bill C-65, be amended in Clause 7 by striking out line 30 at page 5 and substituting the following therefor:
"with pay and benefits."
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in support of this important motion which would amend the provisions of the RCMP Act to ensure that in circumstances in which a member is suspended from duty, that suspension will be with pay and benefits. Clearly the circumstances in which members of the RCMP are suspended are rare. However, in those circumstances it would seem to me that we should recognize the implications of suspension without pay, particularly when that suspension may last for several months or, in some cases, for more than a year. This can cause grave hardship for the individual involved. At the end of the process he could be found to be completely innocent of any wrongdoing. He may very well have had to give up his home and perhaps be unable to afford legal counsel because he has no income.
The committee which studied this legislation with care heard strong representations from both the Association of 17 Divisions and the divisional representatives on this important point.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to emphasize that the Association and the RCMP Division Staff Relations Representatives were unanimous in their contention that suspensions without pay are not required to ensure the sound administration of the RCMP. They were unanimous. Mr. Speaker, these people are elected by RCMP members throughout Canada to defend their interests.
As well, Mr. Speaker, I might point out that the Association of 17 Divisions, based in Quebec but with members in all regions of Canada, is made up of some 2,800 members of the RCMP, and this organization also supports the motion.

Mr. Speaker, there are at least five reasons to support this motion. First of all, just like any other Canadian citizen, a member of the RCMP is presumed to be innocent until found guilty. If he is presumed to be innocent, it is unfair that he be suspended without pay and benefits.

I would note that suspension with pay during an investigation into an alleged offence is an acceptable administrative process and was recommended by the Marin Commission. You will recall that Commission reported to the Government in 1976 after having carefully studied all aspects of this question. At page 154 of the Report is found the following:
During a criminal investigation or a service investigation of a serious nature and any subsequent proceedings, a member should be either suspended with pay or assigned to other duties.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, I would note that suspension without pay, in effect, presupposes guilt and constitutes immediate punishment. Suspension without pay is perceived as exerting extreme pressure, in many cases, on the member to resign, thus denying the member a proper hearing.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, to those who argue that it is not fair to keep a member on the force if he or she is accused of having committed serious wrong-doing, I would note that a member who is alleged to have committed a very serious wrong-doing or a criminal offence, and whose services can no longer be accepted within the force, can be processed for discharge on an urgent basis. Clearly such discharges would be rare indeed, Mr. Speaker. I would hope that the Government will recognize the injustice of the proposal in the Bill and will accept the unanimous representation of the divisional representatives on this question as well as the strong views expressed by the Association of 17 Divisions.

Mr. Speaker, I hope that after consideration of this motion the Government will accept it so that justice will be done to all members of the RCMP.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, I want to support this amendment very strongly. I moved a similar amendment to the Bill when it was in committee. I have a very strong interest in this issue because, as Minister, I appointed the Marin Commission in the 1970s. The recommendation that members of the force should not be suspended without pay and benefits was one of the recommendations of the Marin Commission.
As my hon. colleague pointed out, this sort of treatment of members of the force is really in contradiction to our Canadian Charter of Rights whereby an individual is considered to be innocent until proven guilty. It is contrary to many other basic principles of justice. I will not prolong the debate, but I feel this is an amendment that should be accepted by the Government if it wants to respect the principles of the constitution and the principles that are inherent in our dealings with
employees and our labour relations policy generally. 1 urge the Minister to give serious consideration to this amendment and to accept it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I clearly would not dismiss lightly any recommendation made by Judge Rene Marin in his report. 1 happen to be a good friend of Judge Marin. I am a supporter of his and 1 worked with him at the Canada Post Corporation. He is the chairman of that corporation and a very highly regarded individual who produced an excellent report.
I think it is appropriate for us to look at the proposal that is being made by my colleague, the Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), which is flawed in at least two regards. One is a policy matter, and the other is the structure of the amendment that he is proposing.
Section 13.1 of the Act presently reads:
Every member who has contravened, is found contravening, or is suspected of contravening the code of conduct or an Act of Parliament or of the legislature of any province, may be suspended from duty by the Commissioner.
What would be the effect of the amendment proposed by my hon. friend across the way? My hon. friend would remove the words "by the Commissioner" and substitute for that the following: "with pay and benefits".
The first concern that Members of the House should have is a technical concern. I do not understand why the Hon. Member for Burnaby would propose to strip away from the Commissioner the right to make any suspension. That is not at all clear to me from the Hon. Member's amendment. By removing the individual who has the authority to make the suspension and specifying no one, how is the interest of the member served? Is he suggesting that no one within the force has the authority to suspend a member with or without pay, or is he suggesting that the authority to suspend a member with or without pay should be broadened and should be conferred on a broader category of individuals than just the Commissioner?
I suggest to the Hon. Member that if he is concerned about the welfare, the well-being, and the feelings of members of the force, surely the rank and file members of the force would be interested in hearing from him why he would take away an authority which is vested in one individual, the head of the organization, and leave us in a position where, presumably, the effect would be to simply broaden the authority to suspend a member. What is the reason for this sort of amendment?
There is also a policy consideration here, Mr. Speaker. I listened with interest to my colleagues arguing in favour of the principle that when members of the force are suspended they should be suspended with pay as opposed to without pay. Indeed, the committee looked at this when the matter was before it and the committee decided to reject the amendment which has been proposed.
There are a number of reasons for that. The first is that in the majority of cases where an individual is suspended, he is suspended with pay. It is perhaps appropriate to do that. However, there are some instances where an offence which has
February 5, 1986

been alleged is so serious that it would be appropriate to suspend a member without pay. For example, if a member of the force is charged with bank robbery and there is photographic evidence, then there is the potential that over a protracted period of time the officer could find himself in court charged with a serious criminal offence with sufficient evidence to merit suspending him from his duties. Yet, he would continue to be paid during that period if the Hon. Member's amendment were to pass.
This raises questions about the appropriateness of this sort of action and whether or not it brings the administration of justice into disrepute. Our concern is that nothing should be done which would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.
If the Hon. Member for Burnaby and the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) want to make an argument in terms of whether or not there is a presupposition that an individual is guilty, they could logically extend that argument to being one against suspension either with or without pay. They would make the argument that surely the court will decide whether the individual who is charged under the Criminal Code is guilty or not guilty and it is not up to the RCMP to suspend the individual at all. However, they are not arguing that. They are saying that it is appropriate, even before a conviction has been secured, for the force to suspend an individual in some cases. The only issues in dispute here are who will do the suspension and whether the suspension should be with or without pay.
There are a couple of other points I would like to make as well, Mr. Speaker. I think the Hon. Member would be concerned about the possibility of creating a special class for the RCMP with privileges and rights which extend beyond those which are granted by Parliament to other public employees. When other public employees in the public service are suspended, the authority is there to suspend them without pay under some circumstances. Yet, the effect of the Hon. Member's amendment would be to create a privileged class in this instance and to confer benefits on members of the RCMP which simply are not conferred upon other federal employees.
I suggest that that sort of double standard would be unfair.
There is one other point that I would like to make before sitting down, Mr. Speaker. I gave the members of the committee the assurance that we would bring in amendments to the regulations that would ensure that any suspension of pay of a member is grievable and that, if there is an injustice being done by the administrative action, the member would have the authority to grieve and take advantage of the various provisions under the regulations. We intend to keep that commitment and to ensure that rights of members of the force are protected.
However, we do not believe that a privileged group should be set up with special rights and privileges not conferred on other public employees. We do not believe that any action should be taken by Parliament which would have the effect of bringing the administration of justice into disrepute.
RCMP Act

Mr. Speaker, 1 have listened with a good deal of interest to the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty). What he refuses to recognize is that for many years now there has been a feeling among many people, and members of the force in particular, that the RCMP is a law unto itself, that the rules under which it operates were modeled after the rules and laws of the armed forces of the 17th or 18th century.
Before I proceed to the comments I want to make, 1 will deal with one point which the Minister made a few moments ago. He said that if we do this for the RCMP we will have two classes of public employees, that these people will have conditions which do not apply to all other public servants. I suggest the fact is the exact opposite, because all other public sevants except employees on Parliament Hill have the right by law to belong to unions, whether it is the Public Service Alliance or the Professional Institute. When they are accused of wrongdoing or disciplined by suspension or firing, they have a right to ask their unions to grieve on their behalf and deal with it through a number of steps.
However, the RCMP force has no organization and the Commissioner does not want them to have one. The Minister and the Government agree with the Commissioner, so that when the Commissioner or senior officials in the RCMP believe that an ordinary member of the force has done wrong, the Commissioner shall be the prosecutor, the judge and jury to decide on the penalty. That is unacceptable.
Let me briefly cite for the record the views expressed in a very fine presentation on this subject by the committee of seventeen. They say:
Our reasons for recommending that a member be suspended with pay and allowances are as follows:
1.	The Constitution Act, 1982, presumes every person to be innocent until proven guilty by due process of law.
The RCMP Commissioner wants the exact opposite. When he suspends an officer without pay he has already made a judgment. There is no due process of law or consideration by a committee of peers or outside supervisory group. The committee goes on to state:
2.	Suspension from duty with pay pending completion of an investigation for an alleged offence or a breach of the Code of Conduct is an acceptable administrative process. This was a recommendation of the Marin Commission.
The Minister says he is proud of his friendship with the Marin Commission, but he is quite prepared to ignore Justice Marin's recommendation when it does not suit him. The committee goes on to state:
3.	Suspension from duty without pay presupposes guilt and may constitute immediate punishment before due process of law has been completed.
4.	Suspension from duty without pay is perceived as exerting extreme pressure on a member to resign from the Force.
They go on to describe an actual case of an officer who was suspended without pay. Fortunately, the Commissioner subsequently agreed that the officer should be paid while he was

suspended. However, it took two and a half years until the case was finally settled. The Committee states:
In view of the fact that current proceedings are lengthy, most in excess of two years, it may be realistic to conclude that the member will not be in a financial position to contest the discharge proceedings.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a brief intervention in this debate on this amendment. I am not a former Solicitor General like the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. All-mand), but I did spend some pleasurable time as a Crown attorney and defence counsel in Vancouver. I have called RCMP officers as witnesses for my cases and I have cross-examined them in other cases, so I believe I have some experience with these officers in their day-to-day work.
I believe they should receive salary and benefits while under suspension. I suggest that the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) is not considering this issue in human terms. I might say that he is a bit too stuffy when he says this brings the administration of justice into dispute.
Disrepute.
That it brings the administration of justice into disrepute. That is a rather high-sounding principle but it does not mean anything in the context of this very human situation.
It does to me.

It is a very high-sounding principle. Let us consider the human situation. These officers are very special and have a very difficult job. There is a greater possibility for them to get into trouble than the average public servant. I make the case that it is a rather unique job and if special cases must be made for them, let us do so. It will not set a precedent for the whole public service.
As my colleagues have pointed out, the civil service has a better grievance procedure and union protection. Let us look at it in the context of human terms and the special job that these police officers must perform. If there is an allegation by which they can be suspended, they are helpless. They are not rich people but ordinary Canadians with families. They cannot afford to hire expensive lawyers to help them when they are under suspension.
The Hon. Solicitor General pays great tribute to Justice Marin and his report. Why do you not follow the report if you have such great respect for the judge, because he clearly saw the human side of the issue? With respect, the Minister ducks behind the technicalities. I believe that these technicalities can easily be rectified and I wish to propose a subamendment to the amendment by my hon. friend, the Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald):
That Bill C-65, be amended in Clause 7 by striking out line 30 at page 5 and substituting the following therefor:
"by the Commissioner, with pay and benefits".
The Commissioner can still apply the suspension but it will be with pay and benefits. The Minister would not be able to duck behind that technicality.
I ask the Minister to consider the human terms because these people face special and difficult circumstances. It is easier for them, compared to other public servants, to get into trouble but they are left unprotected. It would be no detriment to the Government to exercise some human kindness and allow for suspension with pay and benefits. There is a principle which we must take into consideration besides the money that such a provision would cost, and I suspect that Conservative back-benchers would agree, if they were here listening to what I just said. I ask the Solicitor General to consider this subamendment.

Mr. Speaker, during the submissions of the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) he said: "Nothing should be done to bring the administration of justice into disrepute". If there is anything that would bring the administration of justice into disrepute, it is the presumption of guilt before a fair hearing by a particular tribunal.
I cannot help but point out the hypocrisy in the position of the Solicitor General. When he was the Minister of National Revenue, he put together what was known as the Declaration of Taxpayer Rights. I am sure you recall when he put that out, Mr. Speaker. He said that henceforth the taxpayers of Canada would have certain rights and he proceeded to point out what those rights are.
One of those rights, and this is a document put out by the Solicitor General when he was the Minister of National Revenue, was the presumption of honesty. He said: "You are entitled to be presumed honest unless there is evidence to the contrary". He went on to say that "you are entitled to every benefit allowed by the law".
One could ask the Solicitor General why taxpayers should be allowed every benefit allowed by the law yet members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police not be entitled to every benefit allowed by the law? The law of Canada is the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms which states at Clause 1 \(d) that a resident of Canada:
to be presumed innocent until proven guilty according to law in a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal.
The Solicitor General says nothing should be done to bring the administration of Justice into disrepute. His position of not allowing members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to be suspended with full pay and benefits brings the administration of justice into disrepute because it presumes that an officer is guilty of some offence. Why else would you suspend an officer without pay? One could conclude that by suspending

A person is presumed and assumed innocent, regardless of the evidence prior to a trial. Yet the Solicitor General is suggesting that in the case of someone charged with bank robbery he or she should be suspended without full pay and benefits. Is the Solicitor General not saying that the commissioner, in this particular case, has the authority to condemn an officer or a member of the Force who is still innovent according to the law of Canada? It is a basic and fundamental principle of our justice system that one is presumed innocent until proven guilty. I cannot understand why the Solicitor General is so adamant in his position that he wants to suspend members of the Force without pay and benefits.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) and other Hon. Members have indicated why an individual should not be suspended without full pay and benefits. We in the Official Opposition believe-and I am sure the NDP would agree- that all members who are in the midst of an investigation should be suspended with full pay and benefits or assigned to other duties. Otherwise, the person is being convicted before he or she is given a fair hearing, before the person's final guilt is determined. It is a preliminary finding of guilt if the person is suspended. It is not only contrary to the basis of the justice system in Canada, but on humanitarian and compassionate grounds, and on those grounds alone, one could argue that a member of the Force should not be suspended without full pay and benefits and that indeed one should be suspended with full pay and benefits.
Can we imagine the hardship involved for a member of the Force who is suspended without full pay and is subjected to a long hearing or investigation? Let us say that it takes from six months to a year before the RCMP conducts its own investigation into a particular allegation. What is the particular member who is presumed innocent supposed to do? He or she is denied full pay and benefits. Presumably some of the benefits are for the member's family, so the family suffers as a result. Is he or she to go on welfare? Is he or she to go on unemployment insurance? We can see how serious the matter is, if the commissioner is allowed to suspend an individual without full pay and benefits.
After the final determination of the particular allegation, if the person is found to have contravened the code of conduct or the Criminal Code of Canada, after he or she has been found guilty, we all agree that then and only then should the commissioner be allowed to suspend the person without pay. What has changed his mind since he was made the Solicitor General of Canada? Why should RCMP officers and members not be afforded the same rights as any other Canadian is afforded? Mr. Speaker, at committee we had the benefit of listening to RCMP divisional staff relations representatives in respect of their views on Bill C-65, an Act to amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act. On behalf of the Internal Affairs Committee, RCMP divisional staff relations representatives presented a brief to the committee. One could conclude, therefore, given the fact that it was the first item they raised, that it is one of the most important, if not the most important, concerns of the RCMP divisional staff relations representatives in respect of the Bill. It is obvious why this would be a very serious concern.
I should like to quote from the particular submission. They started off by saying:
The question of whether the Commissioner of the RCMP needs the authority to suspend a member of the force without pay has been a major issue for discussion since 1973.
They referred to an administrative bulletin which was issued last year and said:
Prior to the passage of this regulation, the commissioner did not have clear authority for suspension without pay. The RCMP divisional staff relations representatives unanimously feel that suspension without pay is not necessary for the proper administration of the force.
They gave their reasons for saying it.
It goes on to list five important reasons why a member of the Force should not be suspended without pay and, if anything, should be suspended with full pay and benefits. First, they say that a member of the RCMP is a Canadian citizen and as such is presumed innocent until proven guilty by due process, the point 1 raised earlier. The second point they raise is that suspension with pay during an investigation into an alleged offence is an acceptable administrative process as recommended by the Marin Commission.
The Marin Commission spoke about this very issue and recommended that during a criminal investigation or service investigation of a serious nature, and any subsequent proceed-

ings, a member should be either suspended with pay or assigned to other duties.
The commission also recommended that no more than 45 days should normally elapse between the commencement and termination of any service investigation, and that if the investigation cannot be concluded within that time the member should be advised of his position and of the current status of the investigation.
The Marin Commission spent a lot of time putting this report together. As you know, Mr. Speaker, as you were a Member of the House at the time, the commission was instituted by the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) who was then Solicitor General. The Solicitor General has dismissed these recommendations in a very frivolous manner without giving good solid reasons why an officer should not be suspended with full pay and benefits. He cited the example of the bank robber, but that is just not good enough.
The third item raised by the representatives of the RCMP at committee was that suspension without pay presupposes guilt and constitutes immediate punishment. Once again, authority is being given to the Commissioner of the RCMP to be investigator, prosecutor and executioner all at the same time and that is not fair.
The fourth item raised by the representatives is that suspension without pay is perceived as exerting extreme pressure on a member to resign, thus denying a proper hearing. If one is charged with a criminal offence, one is presumed innocent until proven guilty. I suppose if there was a case of continual insubordination, that might be a reason to suspend an officer. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if you look at the conflict of interest regulations which involve Members of Parliament, members of the Cabinet and other federal appointees, you will find that the conflict of interest regulations relate to their present activities. As the Bill is now worded there could only be review under Section 28 of the Federal Court Act, a fairly narrow review. Those members do have the right to review under Section 18 as well as Section 28 of the Federal Court Act.
The net effect of these four motions would be to enhance the protection of members of the RCMP during the grievance process, once again bearing in mind the fact that the Government still refuses to grant to members of the RCMP the basic rights to which all other Canadians are entitled, namely the right to full collective bargaining and freedom of association.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do however think we should applaud my hon. friend's artistry and ingenuity in doing that.
I would like to comment briefly on these four motions. Motion No. 3 purports to provide for group grievances in addition to individual grievances. Group grievances are possible at the present time. Grievances on the same issue which are filed by a number of members would be consolidated by the Force if practicable. The issue here is whether a class grievance on behalf of a number of members of the force should be able to be filed. The concern which the Government has is that it wants to do whatever it can to avoid a situation where one member of the Force, purporting to speak on behalf of a number of his colleagues, files a grievance when, in fact, he does not speak on their behalf. It is for this reason that we cannot support Motion No. 3.
February 5, 1986

Motion No. 4 provides that each level in the grievance process should render a decision within 30 days. We believe that at the same time as pressure is put and should be put on the system to ensure that decisions are taken as rapidly as possible, we should also not create arbitrary deadlines which, in some cases, simply could not be met. Clause 46(2) of the Bill provides that all proceedings before a board must be dealt with expeditiously. There may be some instances where it is simply impossible to deal with a particular grievance within 30 days. As a consequence, it would possibly be doing an injustice to the individual involved if a decision were forced in less than that period of time. That is why it is important to allow sufficient flexibility for the system to work properly.
The issue in Motion No. 6 is a highly technical one. It is whether or not it is necessary, as proposed by my hon. colleague from Burnaby, that wherever a review is permitted of the Commissioner's decision under Section 28 of the Federal Court Act, review should also be explicitly provided for under Section 18 of that Act.
The Government has looked at this and feels that the provision in question relates to the right of a member to appeal the final decision of the Commissioner to the Federal Court of Appeal. Second, under the Federal Court Act there are two avenues for appeal, the first through Section 18 and the second through Section 28. Section 18 provides for appeals to the Federal Court Trial Division of decisions of an administrative body and/or interlocutory motions such as mandamus, certiorari, etc. Section 28 provides for appeals to the Federal Court of Appeal of decisions made on a judicial or a quasi-judicial basis.
An appeal from the Commissioner's decisions, because they are judicial or quasi-judicial in nature, accordingly, must be brought before the Federal Court of Appeal pursuant to Section 28. It would be legally contradictory to provide for an appeal of the Commissioner's decision under both Section 18 and Section 28 of the Federal Court Act given the varying nature of appeals provided for under these sections.
The fact that Bill C-65 is silent with respect to a Section 18 appeal does not preclude a motion under that section from being Filed when it is appropiate, for example, when a purely administrative issue is to be determined. For that reason, the proposal that is made by the Hon. Member is redundant and unnecessary in this particular case. On the other hand, specifically providing a reference to Section 18 in this section, dealing with appeals from the Commissioner's decisions, would not only be legally incorrect but would also undoubtedly mislead some members into launching an appeal under this section. Accordingly, in order to avoid members using the wrong appeal provision, reference to Section 18 has been deliberately left out.
Finally, the issue with regard to Motion No. 7 is whether the Governor in Council, rather than the Commissioner, should make regulations governing the presentation and consideration of grievances. It is the Commissioner who is charged with the control and management of the force. The grievance
RCMP Act
system is an integral part of the internal management of the Force, and to divest the Commissioner of the power to make rules respecting the representation and consideration of grievances would be to dilute his control and management of the Force.
Having the Commissioner make rules governing the grievance process in entirely consistent with the general principle that a body normally seized with a judicial or quasi-judicial function makes its own rules regulating the proceedings before it. For example, the Federal Court Act and the Supreme Court Act provide for these judicial bodies to make their own rules of practice and procedure. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, the committee and the members of the Government felt that the procedures in the Bill today are the correct procedures.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to restrict my comments to Motion No. 4 with respect to the time period. The motion moved by the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) would amend Section 31(6) to read as follows: "as soon as possible after the presentation and consideration of a grievance at any level in the grievance process, and in any event, within 30 days the member constituting the level shall render a decision". The operative words are: "in any event, within 30 days".
This particular amendment is suggested to put a timeframe on the grievance procedure and, in my view, relatives to Motion No. 1. We spent a considerable amount of time dealing with that motion which deals with a member of the Force being suspended. It was my submission, and that of the Official Opposition, that a member of the Force should be suspended with full pay and benefits for the reasons I gave earlier.
As I pointed out in my earlier submissions, on page 154 of the Marin Commission it is recommended:
During a criminal investigation or a service investigation of a serious nature and any subsequent proceedings, a member should be either suspended with pay or assigned to other duties.
In his so-called wisdom the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) decided not to adopt this particular suggestion by the Marin Commission, which recommendation was a good one. I hope the Solicitor General will continue to rethink his position. I am sure that reason will prevail in the long run.
However, if, after serious deliberations, the Solicitor General decides that he will not agree to suspending a member of the RCMP with full pay and benefits and affording a member the same rights as any other Canadian, surely he will consider limiting the period within which the RCMP can investigate a particular complaint.
The Solicitor General went over Motion No. 4 rather quickly. He dismissed it almost summarily, I would suggest. He indicated that he did not want to put any impediment in the way which may affect the investigation of a particular alleged offence. What is needed is some method through which those who are conducting the investigation within the RCMP can move a little faster. We all know how slow an investigation could be in certain cases. The investigation can be speeded up

February 5, 1986

or slowed down depending upon certain circumstances that should not, in my view, be taken into consideration.
If you impose a time period and tell the invetigating body that it must report within the given limited period, that particular step in the procedure will be completed within that time. However, if you do not set out a time, the steps may take weeks, months, or perhaps even years while the officer is suspended without full pay and benefits. You are nodding your head in agreement, Mr. Speaker, and I know that you agree with me. If you were given the opportunity you would make submissions to support what I am saying.
In the portion of the Marin Commission dealing with suspension with pay and benefits it says:
No more than 45 days should normally elapse between the commencement and termination of any service investigation. If the investigation cannot be concluded within that time, the member should be advised of his position and of the current status of the investigation.
That is pretty reasonable, Mr. Speaker, and I see that you are nodding your head again in agreement. It seems that you are agreeing with everything I am saying here today. I would only hope that given the position you occupy in this House you might somehow persuade your junior, the Solicitor General, to see it our way, as well. I cannot understand why the Solicitor General will not agree to at least the Marin Commission recommendation which provides for a time limit of 45 days.
If the investigation cannot be completed within 45 days, Commissioner Marin suggested that the member should be advised of his position and the current status of the investigation. That is all that is being recommended. It is not being said that if the investigation cannot be completed within 45 days it should be terminated. It is being said that if you cannot do it within 45 days you must advise the member of the status and position of the investigation. I suggest that the principles of natural justice would demand that a limitation period be put on the investigation. Any person who is under suspicion and alleged to have committed a breach of the code of conduct or the Criminal Code of Canada is entitled to an investigation and a hearing within a reasonable period of time.
That is another basic and fundamental principle of our criminal justice system. Section 7 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms deals with legal rights. I will not take the time of the House to read it but it says that an accused person is entitled to a trial within a reasonable period of time.
I suggest that Mr. Justice Marin's time period or the 30-day period suggested by the Member for Burnaby is a reasonable time within which the RCMP should complete its investigation.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this important motion would implement a recommendation which was made by the Marin Commission in 1976, to which there has been previous reference, and by the McDonald Commission which reported some years later. The Marin Commission recommended that the definition of complaint be the following: "Any communication received from a member of the public either orally or in writing which criticizes the behaviour of a member of the Force or alleges the failure of the Force itself to meet public expectations".

Another example would be a case in which members of a group in a small community might feel that inadequate resources had been allocated to their community. It is not a complaint about a specific member but nevertheless it is a complaint which should be reviewed by the Public Complaints Commission. This amendment would enable them to complain about these matters.
Another illustration of the kind of complaint which could be brought if this amendment were adopted but could not be brought if the wording of the Bill remains as proposed by the Government, is a complaint with respect to hiring policies. I had the honour to serve as a member of the Special Subcommittee on Equality Rights. One of the issues that came before that subcommittee was the hiring policy of the RCMP and its policy with respect to individuals who happen to be gay or lesbian.
I remind the House that the committee was made up of five Conservative Members of Parliament from different provinces in Canada, one Liberal and one New Democrat. The equality rights subcommittee unanimously recommended to the Government that the hiring policies of the RCMP be amended and that qualified men and women not be denied the right to join the RCMP solely on the basis of their sexual orientation but should be judged on their merits as all other applicants are judged.
This amendment would allow members of the public who are concerned about that hiring policy to make submissions to the Public Complaints Commission. We can hope, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps the Government, in responding to the unanimous recommendations of the equality of rights subcommittee on February 25, will implement that important recommendation and ensure that equality is a reality for all Canadians and is not denied to those who happen to be gay or lesbian.
In the event that that important recommendation is rejected by the Government, then surely it should be open to members of the public to complain about those neanderthal and destructive hiring policies of the RCMP. The purpose of this amendment is to allow that kind of policy issue to be dealt with by the Public Complaints Commission.
We have heard from the Commissioner of the RCMP his reasons for opposing this suggestion. I would hope the enlightened Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) might recognize that his colleagues on the equality rights committee were persuaded that the current policies of the RCMP are unjust and must be repealed.
The wording of the amendment in question is very much the wording of the original Act in 1978. In 1978, Bill C-50, one of the many predecessor Bills to this legislation, stated that any person having a complaint concerning the activities of the Force in general or the conduct of any member in particular may make a complaint to the Public Complaints Commission.

Mr. Speaker, I will speak briefly to this motion. The Opposition has always supported an expanded definition of a complaint for reasons that were indicated at committee. 1 do not believe there is any necessity to reiterate arguments I made at committee with respect to why we should have an expanded definition of what a complaint is.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Bill before Parliament today establishes an independent public complaint system or structure. The very guts of this new creation is a definition of what constitutes a complaint. In order to set the machinery in action, you need a complaint.
The Government in its at times questionable wisdom decided to provide a particular definition of complaint. It says that any member of the public having a complaint concerning the conduct in the performance of any duty or function under this Act of any member or other persons appointed or employed under the authority of this Act, whether or not that member of the public is affected by the subject matter of the complaint, may make the complaint to, and it goes on to list how a particular individual can file a complaint.
It certainly provides for third-party complaints. It says: "Whether or not the member of the public is affected by the subject matter of the complaint". If you have an RCMP officer punching someone in the nose, the victim does not necessarily have to complain. Someone who saw the incident, or any other person, could complain of the conduct. To allow third party complaints is a step in the right direction.
The restriction causes considerable concern. The complaint has to concern the conduct in the performance of any duty or function under the Act. As was pointed out previously, it does not allow for a member of the public to complain generally about RCMP policy with regard to any particular matter.
I would like to quote again from the report of the Commission of Inquiry relating to public complaints. I referred to it previously as the Marin Report. It provides for a more expanded definition of complaint.
The Marin Report recommends that a complaints system be set up that would essentially be remedial in nature. At page 73 we find:
A public complaint system is remedial when it emphasizes the positive aspects of corrective action and encourages the use of other-than-punitive measures to achieve a change in individual behaviour or performance. Such a system will make possible the identification of changes that are necessary and which affect groups or members of the Force as a whole in response to public complaints.
On page 74 the following is found:
We must begin with a definition of "public complaint" sufficiently comprehensive-

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police should adopt as their definition of a complaint the following: "Any communication received from a member of the public, either orally or in writing, which criticizes the behaviour of a member of the Force or alleges the failure of the Force itself to meet public expectations".
We all agree that one should be entitled to complain about the conduct of a particular member of the Force. Where we disagree is whether the public can complain or allege the failure of the Force itself to meet public expectations. Surely the public should have a right to complain specifically about certain policies of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) no doubt would argue, "Well, I am in charge. I will make sure that policies are developed and rules are followed that are in the best interests of Canadians in Canada generally". That would suggest an opinion of himself that perhaps is undeserved.

I do not know whether Canadians or I- given the Solicitor General's track record with respect to other very reasonable amendments to this legislation-would put our faith in the Solicitor General to ensure that practices are followed in keeping with the best interests of Canadians and that meet public expectations. The Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) cited certain situations that might arise that should provide for triggering the complaint mechanism as provided in Bill C-65. I would like to advance one further situation. It was a situation that we in this House dealt with last week concerning certain allegations of sexual harassment by members within the Force. We all know of a newspaper article that originated in British Columbia which alleged that six members of the RCMP had indicated to a particular officer that there was harassment of sorts within a detachment.
We asked the Solicitor General to initiate an external investigation of the complaints. He refused. We indicated how we felt about that refusal in this House and elsewhere.

Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) and I were prompted to do so by the inaction of the Government with respect to what we considered to be very serious allegations.
RCMP Act
The Solicitor General, speaking for the Government of Canada, decided that it would allow the Force to investigate itself and that it had full faith and confidence that the investigation would be conducted with dispatch and in an objective fashion, notwithstanding that the Force would be investigating itself, notwithstanding that the allegations appeared to be widespread. Obviously the Commissioner of the RCMP got to the Solicitor General. It appears that the Solicitor General often marches to the tune of the Commissioner of the RCMP. The evidence was there to suggest the very serious problem in respect of the role of women in the RCMP. Mr. Speaker, in considering Motion No. 9, a motion to amend a new procedure which is being introduced by this Bill, the RCMP public complaints procedure, it seems to me that we should look back to the root of this procedure to see why it is being recommended in the first place. The first police public complaints procedure established in Canada was established in Metropolitan Toronto in the late 1970s. It came about after an incident which occurred in Toronto that caused a great furor, and that was, the shooting of a black man named Buddy Evans by a police officer on the Metropolitan Toronto Police Force.
As a result of the shooting and the subsequent coroner's investigation, racial tensions in Metropolitan Toronto virtually exploded. It was a very tense period of time. People were demonstrating throughout the city. Great crowds were coming before Toronto City Council and various municipal councils in Metropolitan Toronto and great demonstrations were going on in Nathan Phillips Square. In an effort to work out a solution to this situation, the Attorney General of the Province of Ontario proposed a procedure that had been adopted and utilized in some parts of the United States previously, and that was, the citizens' complaint procedure.
This procedure was introduced after a good deal of discussion and negotiation with the various community groups in Metropolitan Toronto, the Police Department, the Police Commission, municipal councillors and the provincial Government. In introducing this procedure, a negotiation occurred in an attempt to balance off the concerns of the citizens and the concerns of the Police Department. There were competing interests and concerns. There was the concern on the part of

February 5, 1986
RCMP Act
the public that police officers could do whatever they wanted to do, but there was the concern on the part of police officers that they could very well be shafted by this whole process and be wronged unjustly.
The procedure that was worked out is the same procedure that appears in this Bill, a procedure in which individual complaints dealing with individual officers may be brought before a complaint board to be dealt with and solved on an individual basis and not on a policy basis. It was not an attempt to pillory the entire Police Department or to introduce some procedure whereby one could debate policy. It was simply designed to deal with individual police complaints. That is the procedure that is before us today and it seems to me that that is the procedure we should adopt rather than considering the amendment that has been put forward by the Hon. Member for Burnaby.
If we consider the Hon. Member's amendment, we will tamper with the entire theory of the complaint procedure. We will tamper with the confidence the police and individual citizens have in the procedure. If we destroy that confidence, we will destroy all benefit of this procedure. It has been proven in the past, and certainly in Metropolitan Toronto, that this procedure has solved a really serious problem. We have before us a mechanism by which we can head off serious problems which may occur with the RCMP, and I think we should certainly adopt the Bill as put before us and reject the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment put by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). I would like to deal with two or three reasons for my support.
Let me begin with the question of hiring practices. In my time here, I have supported the concept that Canada is bilingual and I have supported the proposals put by the former and present Governments to encourage more Fracophones to become members of the federal Public Service. I cannot say the same of all Manitoba Members of Parliament who sit on the government side.
I received a complaint recently from one of my consistitu-ents. At a time when the RCMP is encouraging applications and hiring people, he applied to become a member of the RCMP. He met all the qualifications except for one. The RCMP was engaged in an effort to increase the number and percentage of Francophone members of the Force.
I made inquiries about this matter and found that the situation is quite an interesting and complicated one. In Ontario and Quebec, the Provinces of Canada which are the largest in size and population, there are provincial police forces and therefore the RCMP plays a relatively limited role in those two provinces. It deals only with matters which comes under federal jurisdiction. However, in all the other provinces, and particularly in the rural areas, the provinces contract with the RCMP to do all the regular police work.
Many people, not just in Manitoba but in other provinces I am sure, are concerned about the policy of the RCMP to increase rapidly the number of Francophone members.
Although roughly 30 per cent of the country's population is Francophone, in terms of the policing which the RCMP carries out in the eight provinces and the territories, the Francophone population is very small. I am not saying they are wrong. I am saying that it was a legitimate question asked by my constituents. It was a difficult problem for me to try to think through. I think it would be helpful for the RCMP, and for the people of Canada, to have an independent review committee look at this type of problem, and not having necessarily to wait for an invidual person to make a complaint.
I would now like to deal with two other matters. I recognize there is a problem with respect to drugs. The illegal use, purchase and distribution of drugs is a tremendously complex problem. I do not pretend to be an expert on the matter, or to have an answer as to how this type of problem can be dealt with. However, I can remember not so many years ago when the public, the courts and police forces considered possession of marijuana, for example, much more seriously than it is now considered. It was the belief that the possession and distribution of marijuana should be dealt with in a much more tough way than it is today. I am sure defence lawyers received many complaints concerning allegations that RCMP officers working in the drug field were frequently involved in entrapment. I repeat, I am not an expert on this matter. I am not prepared to say that, perhaps, the RCMP had to do the things which they did at the time. I suggest to the Minister that when this type of problem arises, an independent review board could look at it and lay down some general principles as to the way the Force should deal with the situation. That would be helpful both to the RCMP and to the public in general.
The last illustration I wish to draw is with respect to complaints which frequently arise from Indian reserves in different parts of the country. I am speaking of complaints from individual members of groups of people who live on the reserves who are not satisfied with the treatment they have received from the RCMP. I recognize that there are tremendous problems with alcoholism, and all sorts of other problems which I will not go into, which occur in and around native reserves. I recognize that the police forces which deal with these problems have an extremely difficult task. However, I suggest to the Minister that if some independent board could look at the complaints and lay down some general policies then it would make things much easier for the RCMP. Their activity would be much more acceptable to the public, particularly to the people who feel that they have been mistreated.
Without prolonging the debate, I have tried to give three illustrations which I think have some merit. I think an independent commission, given the powers which my colleague the Hon. Member for Burnaby has suggested they should be given, would be worth-while. This is an amendment which should be accepted by the Government.

Mr. Speaker, I was not planning to participate in this debate in light of the fact that there are some very able representatives here, both from our

However, I was sitting in my office listening to the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) and I felt it was incumbent upon me to come down to the Chamber, not only to set the record straight but to suggest that the Solicitor General in his about-face-and I would call it a complete about-face-with respect to the issue of sexual harassment in the RCMP shows what hypocritical action he has taken with respect to this issue. In fact, it shows how he has twisted his role as Solicitor General to serve his own political ends.
I make this challenge in the full knowledge that the Solicitor General some two weeks ago said that he was so concerned about published reports, which included comments from six women members of the RCMP who were concerned about the possibility of harassment, that he immediately ordered an inquiry. I remember that that was on a Sunday. The Solicitor General said that he wanted this situation investigated immediately, that these were serious charges and he wanted to move ahead with them. Two days later, when he was faced with questions in the House by the Opposition with respect to the question of harassment as it had been placed before the Subcommittee on Equality Rights, not only did he deny the existence of such allegations, and not only did he challenge us to put forward a name, but when a name, which had been provided as part of a public presentation, was submitted in the House he took the unprecedented and, I believe, illegal step of personally contacting that person to determine what that person's actions would be in respect of a general complaint to the Canadian Human Rights Commission. I ask the Minister how he expects the Canadian public to have any faith in his operation of the RCMP if, in fact, he has shown in other cases this same type of abject irresponsibility and, indeed, total disregard for the law as he did in this particular case.
I felt that there was enough evidence for a general complaint to be laid before the Canadian Human Rights Commission. That position has been supported by people such as Doris Anderson, former President of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, who said that individual officers in the RCMP are afraid to speak out. I do not blame them. If I were a woman in the RCMP who was being harassed, I would not want to speak out either because I would not want to put my individual relationship with the force on the line.
Quite clearly, the combination of events, including the press reports and studies which have been conducted by Professor Linden of the University of Manitoba, which study was commissioned by the office of the Solicitor General, points out that the number of women who quit the Force is at least double that of the number of men who quit. It has been pointed out that the women in the Force have very low morale because they do not receive much support when they raise issues. This was pointed out in statements made before the subcommittee which dealt with equality rights. The Minister has refused to conduct an independent inquiry, or even to seek one from the Human Rights Commission. He has stood in his place in the House and said that he called this woman-and he knows of whom we speak-not once but twice. I ask Hon. Members

Of course not.

The Minister knows about what I speak. That phone call was worse than the phone call which was made by the former Solicitor General, which ultimately led to his shuffle out of his position because he had shown himself to be so irresponsible. Elmer MacKay, the former-

The motion deals, Mr. Speaker, with the possibility of an independent review, and quite clearly, when the Solicitor General, has taken the law into his own hands on this issue and has refused to consider any involvement, even from the Canadian Human Rights Commission, with the general problem faced by women in the RCMP he has failed in his responsibility to provide a mechanism for independent review. -and less interested in tampering with justice in the way he has done with this particular case-and I will say it outside the Flouse because I think the phone calls the Minister made to that particular constable were totally beyond the call of his duty-

If the Minister is really concerned about increasing participation of women in the Armed Forces, and if he is interested in looking at issues about the lack of Francophone representation in the Armed Forces-which was raised by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-he will agree that in order to get to the bottom of some of these problems we sometimes need an outside investigation which looks at the general nature of the problem. By tying this particular Bill to individual complaints or third party complaints about a single specific action, the Minister is saying he does not believe that the Canadian Human Rights Commission should have the right to carry on general investigations.
If the Minister believes that women in the Armed Forces, in the RCMP and in other organizations are afraid to speak out, one way of facilitating the search for information in a general way in order to make positive changes would be to allow an independent external investigation. Without that particular external investigation we can continue to expect that those women who face harassment will remain silent. They will not be able to speak out because of the potential difficulties within the promotional system if they do speak out on their individual cases. All of us know that these problems exist. If we really want to get to the bottom of them, then let us provide for an external mechanism which would not only have the power to review internal investigations but also have the power to investigate in an external way.
I believe that is what this amendment calls for and that is why I support it.

Motion No. 11
That Bill C-65, be amended in Clause 15 by striking out lines 7 to 37 at page 58 and substituting the following therefor:

made by the Public Complaints Commission."
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in support of this motion which in many respects goes to the very heart of this Bill. There are two central elements to the legislation which is now before the House. The first, of course, deals with the question of establishing a grievance procedure to ensure that the neanderthal labour policies which are currently the case within the RCMP are at least brought forward somewhat. The Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) still refuses to give the elementary right to full and free collective bargaining and freedom of association, but that is a debate for another day.
This motion deals with the second element of this question, and that is, who will have the final say on complaints made by the public with respect to activities by members of the RCMP, either individually or in a group. I want to read the motion
February 5, 1986

because I believe it sets out very clearly what our recommendation is "The final decision on action with respect to public complaints will be made by the Public Complaints Commission". As the Bill is now worded, it is the Commissioner who has the final word, so a member of the public who feels agrieved, whether on a policy question or an individual grievance, will file that grievance with the Public Complaints Commission. The Public Complaints Commission will investigate and perhaps hold a hearing and then will make a recommendation to the Commissioner. Following that recommendation, the Commissioner can accept or reject the recommendation. I believe that that totally undermines the integrity of this process. We have heard from a number of witnesses on this point. I would remind Hon. Members of the House of the representations which were made by a very distinguished criminal lawyer from Toronto on this particular motion. I am speaking, of course, of Mr. Clay Ruby. He said that the Government's Bill in leaving the final decision on a complaint by a member of the public against a member of the RCMP to be decided by the RCMP itself is completely unacceptable, and I quote:
The independent commission of inquiry can be ignored by the RCMP. Based on their track record of ignoring ministerial directives, the law of the land, the Criminal Code and standards of ordinary decency, this does not give one much room for hopeful expectations.
When will politicians understand that the public is no longer prepared to accept that it is proper, fair or just for a police force to investigate itself and make decisions about what disciplinary action to follow from its own misdeeds?
Of course, Mr. Ruby was referring to the sorry chapter in the history of the RCMP, which was very clearly documented by the McDonald Commission, the incidents of breaches of the law and, in some cases, very serious breaches, by the Security Service Operation Checkmate, for example, involving a series of breaches of criminal law and other federal legislation.
What did the Commissioner of the RCMP do in response to that, Mr. Speaker? He said that there will be no disciplinary action whatsoever. "But even if there is to be disciplinary action", said the Commissioner, "I am not going to tell the public what it is". Surely, in a democratic society that kind of response is not acceptable.
The purpose of this motion is to ensure that at the end of the day, after the complaint has been reviewed by the Public Complaints Commission, after there has been discussion with representatives of the RCMP-perhaps, including the Com-
RCMP Act
missioner-the final decision will be in the hands of the Commission itself. I would note as well that the McDonald Commission very clearly and explicitly opposed the suggestion that it should be the Commissioner of the RCMP who had the final say on complaints. The McDonald Commission stated the following, and I quote:
In this regard, we part company with the strongly held view within the RCMP and other police forces that the final judge in complaint matters should be the head of the force. In Bill C-50, to which we have previously referred, which was introduced in 1978 but not passed, the traditional approach was maintained.
Then it states:
But we feel there cannot be public confidence in the complaint procedure if the final arbiter belongs to the force whose conduct is under review.
Surely, that must be the case. Surely, it is not acceptable that the individual in charge of the Force which is being reviewed, the individual in charge of the Force against which a complaint has been laid by a member of the public, should be the person who, at the end of the day, decides whether or not to accept the recommendations of the Public Complaints Commission on that complaint. That makes a mockery of any motion of independent investigation and review of complaints by the public. It undermines the whole thrust of this important step forward involving review by a Public Complaints Commission.
